summary: This is a backend API endpoint for collecting typo and content feedback reports from a website. It loads configuration from an environment file, sets up CORS security, validates incoming requests using nonce tokens, enforces rate limiting to prevent abuse, deduplicates reports, stores them to disk, and optionally emails the admin when new feedback arrives.

explanations.2: This tells PHP to enforce strict type checking, meaning if you pass the wrong type of data to a function, it will error instead of trying to convert it.
explanations.4: This checks if a .env file exists and loads it as key-value pairs; if it doesn't exist or fails, it defaults to an empty array.
explanations.5: The `parse_ini_file` function reads the .env file into an array, but it might return false on error, so the `?:` operator ensures we always have at least an empty array.
explanations.8: This creates a constant called ADMIN_EMAIL from the environment variables, but if it's not set there, it defaults to an empty string.
explanations.24: If the request is coming from an origin (domain) not in the allowed list, reject it immediately with a 403 Forbidden status.
explanations.30: This tells the browser that cross-origin requests from this specific origin are allowed, enabling the frontend to actually receive the response.
explanations.35: Browser preflight requests use OPTIONS method to check permissions; we respond with 204 (no content) to say 'yes, your request is allowed'.
explanations.40: If the file can't be decoded as JSON, the `?:` operator ensures we return an empty array instead of false.
explanations.44: Opening a file in 'c+' mode creates it if it doesn't exist, and positions us at the beginning so we can read or write.
explanations.46: We acquire an exclusive lock so only one process can read/write this file at a time, preventing race conditions.
explanations.47: We delete all file contents and move back to the start so we can write fresh data.
explanations.55: This converts the input to lowercase, removes any character that isn't a-z, 0-9, hyphen, or slash, then limits it to 200 characters.
explanations.58: The `never` return type means this function always exits and never returns normally — useful for error handlers.
explanations.66: We create a token by hashing the current time window with a secret, so the token is valid for a specific 15-minute window.
explanations.70: We divide the current timestamp by the cooldown seconds to get which 'window' we're in, allowing the nonce to be valid for ~15 minutes.
explanations.71: We check if the submitted nonce matches either the current window or the previous one, allowing a small grace period.
explanations.77: A honeypot field: if the optional 'website' field is filled, assume it's a bot and silently reject by returning empty.
explanations.83: We check that the text is between 3-150 characters and contains no control characters (like null bytes) that might cause problems.
explanations.96: The `compact` function creates an array with keys matching the variable names, so `compact('slug', 'text')` becomes `['slug' => $slug, 'text' => $text]`.
explanations.103: We hash the user's IP with a salt value so we can track their requests without storing their actual IP address.
explanations.107: If we can't get a lock (another process is using the file), we give up rather than waiting, to avoid blocking.
explanations.110: We read the file contents; if it's empty or invalid JSON, default to an empty array.
explanations.112: We either get the existing global request counter or initialize a new one with the current timestamp.
explanations.113: If the current time window has expired (more than 60 seconds have passed), reset the counter.
explanations.114: We increment the global request counter and reject if it exceeds the maximum, preventing a flood from any source.
explanations.118: We filter the hourly timestamps to only keep those from the last hour (3600 seconds), removing old entries.
explanations.121: We create a unique key combining the IP hash and article slug so we can track how many times this person reported issues on this specific article.
explanations.122: Similar to line 118, but for per-article tracking over 24 hours (86400 seconds).
explanations.137: We create a hash of the article slug plus the lowercase text so we can compare reports without storing the exact text twice.
explanations.138: We load all reports for this article and search through them to see if any have the same text hash.
explanations.145: This destructures (unpacks) the fields array into individual variables in one line.
explanations.155: We generate a random 6-byte ID, convert it to hexadecimal characters for readability and safe storage.
explanations.158: The text hash is stored with each report so we can later check if a duplicate report comes in without needing the original text.
explanations.174: We check if enough time has passed since the last notification for this article; if not, skip sending another email.
explanations.196: The `@` suppresses error output from the mail function; we only update the throttle file if the email actually sent.
explanations.207: We compute the nonce for the current time window and send it to the frontend so it can include it in the next request.
explanations.211: If no admin token was configured or the provided token doesn't match, reject with 403 Forbidden.
explanations.220: We parse the JSON body sent in the request; if it's invalid JSON, default to an empty array.
explanations.222: The nonce is required and must be valid; if missing or expired, reject the request.
explanations.225: If fields is empty, the honeypot was triggered, so we silently return success (fooling the bot into thinking we accepted it).
explanations.231: If this exact report already exists, pretend we accepted it but don't store a duplicate.
